**What the Rain Forgets**

When the rain finally arrives, the city breathes with something almost forgiving. It does not shout, not at first. It only presses against the windows like a thousand small, curious fingertips, asking to be let in, and then, when no one answers, it begins to fall.

There is a strange mercy in ordinary weather. People rarely stop to wonder about the exact angle at which a cloud has been unraveling above a river valley, or the way an afternoon wind may have carried moisture from a distant sea and folded it into darkness over rooftops long before sunset. But when the rain starts, the world is briefly made simpler: everything is wet, everything is cool, everything is rinsed. The dust that had gathered on windowsills, on books, on the edges of neglected thoughts, dissolves a little. The light above the clouds softens into gray, then pale blue, then the greenish shine of stone and leaves.

I have always liked the idea that weather forgets. It does not hold grudges against the buildings it washes. It does not remember the name of the tree it strikes at random, nor the exact street where it makes someone drop their bag. Rain is not cruel, though it can be careless. It is only passing.

In the evening, after it has done what it came to do, the streets become mirrors without edges. The city lights are pulled downward into puddles, split into ribbons, flickering each time a car passes slowly enough to preserve the image for a moment. There is something almost ceremonial about it: the reflection is not the thing itself. It is only a rumor of the thing, a half-light that exists where the water remembers the sky.

And I think about all the small things we mistake for solid things. The name we gave to a feeling as a child, before the feeling learned to disguise itself. The promise we made in a season that was not meant to be trusted. The face we looked at once and thought, without evidence, that we would meet again. These things, too, are weather. They arrive, they change the atmosphere of a day, they leave marks on the ground. And then they are gone, except for the dampness they leave behind.

Sometimes I imagine that memory works like rain on a stone. The stone is not ruined by it. It only becomes more itself. A walk through the rain should not always be something to fear. It should be a kind of permission to be unfinished, to be wet at the edges, to carry a heavier coat than necessary and walk through the soft gray world without demanding that it make sense before you reach your door.

That is what I want to say, if I can say it freely: do not mistake a season for a sentence. Do not let one passing cloud decide the whole future of your day. There is weather, and there is the person standing in it. There is what happens, and there is who we become because we were there, with our hands tucked into pockets, watching the puddles multiply, listening to the rain do its quiet, forgetting work.

And when it stops, the air will taste faintly metallic, clean, and new. The windows will be streaked. The ground will be black and glossy, full of small reflections that will vanish before anyone has time to look closely. And you will walk on, maybe with your sleeves rolled up, maybe with your hair still a little damp, carrying inside you the strange lightness that comes after something has been washed away that you did not know you were holding.
